# Background {#sec-background}

## Alzheimer's Disease and Neurodegeneration

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder [@ferretti_sex_2018]. As global populations age, the number of individuals with AD and related dementias is projected to rise from approximately 47 million to over 115 million by 2050, with global dementia costs exceeding US\$818 billion annually [@livingston_dementia_2017]. Because the disease remains incurable and late-stage disease-modifying clinical trials have had high failure rates, identifying and tracking AD in its earliest stages, before severe cognitive decline, is critical [@ferretti_sex_2018; @livingston_dementia_2017].

The neuropathological hallmarks of AD are two co-occurring abnormal protein deposits: amyloid-$\beta$ (A$\beta$) plaques and neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) composed of hyperphosphorylated tau [@jack_hypothetical_2010; @tarasoff-conway_clearance_2015]. A$\beta$ is derived from the proteolytic cleavage of the amyloid precursor protein and accumulates extracellularly, while tau is a microtubule-binding protein that, when hyperphosphorylated, aggregates intracellularly to form NFTs and neuropil threads, disrupting axonal transport [@kobayashi_2024_2026; @tarasoff-conway_clearance_2015]. These proteinopathies are accompanied by neurodegeneration (synaptic loss, neuronal death, and structural brain atrophy) as well as neuroinflammation and glial activation [@jack_hypothetical_2010].

Clinically, AD progresses through a slow, decades-long continuum rather than emerging as a sudden discrete state [@dennis_neuroimaging_2008; @jack_hypothetical_2010]. The disease process begins with a prolonged preclinical phase during which A$\beta$ and tau pathology steadily accumulate without producing cognitive deficits, then transitions through a prodromal stage known as Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), characterized by objective cognitive decline that is noticeable but not yet severe enough to impair independent daily living [@dennis_neuroimaging_2008; @livingston_dementia_2017]. The terminal phase is Alzheimer's dementia, defined by severe, multi-domain cognitive and behavioral impairments that prevent functional independence [@jack_hypothetical_2010; @livingston_dementia_2017].

Historically, AD was diagnosed clinically as a syndromal entity based purely on these observable symptoms. However, to facilitate early detection and standardize research, the National Institute on Aging and Alzheimer's Association (NIA-AA) developed the 2018 AT(N) research framework, which formally shifted the definition of AD from a clinical syndrome to a biological construct defined by _in vivo_ biomarkers of amyloid deposition (A), pathologic tau (T), and neurodegeneration (N) [@jack2018]. This shift acknowledged that clinical syndromes are neither sensitive nor specific enough for accurate diagnosis, as typical AD pathology can exist without symptoms (preclinical AD), and typical dementia symptoms can be caused by non-AD pathologies [@jack2018; @kobayashi_2024_2026].

Building upon this, the updated 2024 NIA-AA criteria extended the research framework into clinical practice, expanding the classification into an $AT_1T_2NISV$ profile in which biological diagnosis relies on Core-1 biomarkers of amyloid pathology (A) and soluble tau ($T_1$), with Core-2 biomarkers of aggregated tau ($T_2$) used for disease staging [@jack_jr_revised_2024]. The updated framework also formally incorporates markers for non-specific neurodegeneration (N), inflammation (I), $\alpha$-synuclein copathology (S), and vascular brain injury (V), acknowledging that late-life cognitive decline often involves multiple co-occurring pathologies [@jack_jr_revised_2024; @kobayashi_2024_2026].

![**Archetypical sequence of biomarker changes in Alzheimer's disease.** (A) The hypothesized temporal ordering of AD biomarkers, with amyloid PET abnormality (A) preceding medial temporal lobe tau (T), neocortical tau, neurodegeneration (N), and cognitive decline (C). (B) The effect of coexisting co-pathologies, which accelerate the onset of neurodegeneration and cognitive symptoms. (C) The effect of cognitive reserve, which delays the clinical expression of disease despite equivalent underlying pathology. From @jack_jr_revised_2024. \textcopyright{} 2024 The Authors. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. No modifications made.](../images/atn_nia-aa.jpg){#fig-atn-framework width=60%}

Within this biological framework, structural MRI markers of neurodegeneration (N) are repositioned as indicators of disease severity and predictors of cognitive decline rather than defining diagnostic features [@jack2018; @jack_jr_revised_2024]. Because structural brain changes closely parallel the clinical expression of the disease, accurate measurement of regional neurodegeneration remains vital for tracking disease progression and evaluating disease-modifying therapies [@jack_hypothetical_2010; @jack_jr_revised_2024]. However, the utility of structural MRI depends on separating disease-related atrophy from normal variation due to age, sex, and head size [@ferretti_sex_2018].

## The Hippocampus: Structure, Function, and Atrophy

The hippocampus is a seahorse-shaped cortical structure located deep within the medial temporal lobe, medial to the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle and posterior to the amygdala [@duvernoy_human_2013; @yushkevich_quantitative_2015]. The hippocampal formation is composed of distinct cytoarchitectonic subfields. These include the dentate gyrus (DG), the cornu ammonis sectors (CA1, CA2, CA3, and CA4), and the subiculum [@yushkevich_quantitative_2015]. Its internal circuitry, including the classic trisynaptic pathway, and its widespread connectivity with the neocortex and limbic system make the hippocampus a highly plastic brain region central to memory, spatial navigation, and relational binding [@eichenbaum2004].

![**Cytoarchitectonic subfields of the hippocampal formation.** Drawing by Santiago Ramón y Cajal (1911) illustrating the major subdivisions of the hippocampus, including the entorhinal cortex (EC), dentate gyrus (DG), cornu ammonis sectors (CA1, CA3), and subiculum (Sub). The inset diagram depicts the trisynaptic circuit: EC $\rightarrow$ DG $\rightarrow$ CA3 $\rightarrow$ CA1 $\rightarrow$ Sub. From _Histologie du Système nerveux de l'Homme et des Vertébrés_ (public domain).](../images/CajalHippocampus.png){#fig-cajal-hippocampus width=65%}

Functionally, the hippocampus is most widely recognized as the primary neural substrate for the encoding, consolidation, and retrieval of episodic and declarative memory [@bettio2017; @eichenbaum2004]. It acts as a relational network, binding disparate elements of an experience (such as objects, actions, and spatial contexts) into a cohesive and flexible memory trace [@eichenbaum2004]. Beyond simple memory retention, specific subfields govern distinct cognitive functions. The dentate gyrus and CA3 regions are specifically critical for spatial navigation and "pattern separation," the computational process of orthogonalizing similar neural inputs to prevent memory interference; structural damage to these areas consequently impairs the ability to distinguish similar events and navigate in space [@eichenbaum2004; @reyes2018].

Beyond memory and cognition, the hippocampus regulates the stress response through the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis: its high density of glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors makes it a central negative-feedback regulator of the physiological stress response, but also renders it vulnerable to chronic cortisol exposure, which induces dendritic retraction, inhibits adult neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus, and leads to volumetric atrophy [@bettio2017; @campbell2004; @videbech2004]. As a result, marked hippocampal volume reduction is a consistent neuroimaging finding across a spectrum of psychiatric conditions, including major depressive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and schizophrenia [@campbell2004; @videbech2004].

Most notably, progressive hippocampal atrophy is an early structural biomarker of AD neurodegeneration. According to the established neuropathological staging of AD, the accumulation of tau neurofibrillary tangles typically initiates in the transentorhinal cortex before severely infiltrating the CA1 subfield and subiculum of the hippocampus, eventually spreading to the wider neocortex [@apostolova2006; @franko2013]. _In vivo_ longitudinal MRI studies mirror this pathological progression, demonstrating that while the healthy aging brain undergoes a gradual hippocampal volume reduction estimated at approximately 1.4% per year, AD pathology significantly accelerates this tissue loss, with patients exhibiting average annual hippocampal atrophy rates of approximately 4.6% to 4.7% [@barnes2009].

The trajectory of this structural decay provides prognostic value across the AD continuum. Individuals in the transitional MCI stage exhibit intermediate annualized atrophy rates (averaging around 2.5% to 3.1%), and the precise rate of hippocampal volume loss reliably predicts which patients with MCI will rapidly convert to clinical Alzheimer's dementia [@franko2013; @jack2000]. Furthermore, high-resolution shape and subfield analyses reveal that this atrophy is not globally uniform; structural deformations localize heavily to the CA1 and subicular zones early in the disease, strongly differentiating stable MCI subjects from those with progressive AD pathology [@apostolova2006; @franko2013].

However, interpreting raw hippocampal volumes is complicated by substantial natural inter-subject variability: up to 25% of healthy young adults possess hippocampal volumes as small as those seen in the average healthy individual aged 60 to 75, making raw cross-sectional volume an imperfect predictor of pathology [@lupien2007]. This variance underscores the need for longitudinal imaging to measure individual trajectories of decline [@jack2000] and for demographically adjusted normative reference models that account for age and sex to differentiate healthy anatomical diversity from pathological brain aging [@nobis2019].

## Lateral Ventricles and Ex-Vacuo Dilation

The ventricular system is a series of interconnected, fluid-filled cavities within the brain that produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid [@brinker_new_2014]. The largest of these cavities, the lateral ventricles, extend throughout the cerebral hemispheres and are subdivided into distinct anatomical regions, including the inferior (or temporal) horns, which project into the medial temporal lobes [@todd_ventricular_2018]. The hippocampus lies medial to this inferior horn, sharing a direct anatomical border with the ventricular space [@schoemaker2019; @zandifar2017]. Because of this close spatial relationship, hippocampal integrity and temporal horn volume are closely linked.

The ventricular cavities are lined by ependymal cells and contain the choroid plexus, a vascularized epithelial structure responsible for producing most of the CSF [@damkier_cerebrospinal_2013]. CSF is secreted at a rate of approximately 500 mL per day in healthy adults, with a total volume of roughly 150 mL maintained at any given time through continuous absorption at the arachnoid granulations [@brinker_new_2014]. Surrounding the lateral ventricles, the periventricular white matter is susceptible to damage from chronic small vessel disease, appearing as white matter hyperintensities (WMH) on T2-weighted and FLAIR MRI sequences [@wardlaw_neuroimaging_2013]. Ventricular enlargement and periventricular WMH burden are frequently correlated, both reflecting the cumulative effects of vascular injury and tissue loss on deep white matter [@appelman_total_2008].

In clinical neuroradiology, ventricular size is commonly assessed using the Evans index, defined as the ratio of the maximum width of the frontal horns to the maximum internal diameter of the skull at the same level [@evans_encephalographic_1942]. An Evans index exceeding 0.30 is conventionally used to define ventriculomegaly and is a key criterion in the clinical diagnosis of normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) [@relkin_diagnosing_2005]. However, automated volumetric segmentation from T1-weighted MRI provides more precise and regionally specific quantification of ventricular size than linear ratio measures, enabling researchers to separately evaluate the frontal horns, body, atrium, occipital horns, and temporal horns of the lateral ventricles [@chou_mapping_2009; @todd_ventricular_2018].

Expansion of the lateral ventricles, termed ventriculomegaly, is a consistent structural feature of the aging brain [@todd_ventricular_2018]. In cognitively healthy older adults, the lateral ventricles expand approximately linearly with age, accelerating after sixty as global brain tissue loss accumulates [@madsen_mapping_2015; @oschwald_brain_2020]. While the lateral ventricles themselves do not play a direct role in cognition, their expansion serves as a non-specific proxy for the structural degradation of surrounding cortical and subcortical tissue [@madsen_mapping_2015; @todd_ventricular_2018].

In neurodegenerative disorders, ventricular enlargement is accelerated by a phenomenon known as _ex-vacuo_ dilation. As brain tissue shrinks, the adjacent ventricular CSF spaces passively expand to fill the vacated volume within the fixed confines of the skull [@apostolova2013; @madsen_mapping_2015]. Because the hippocampus is among the first structures to show severe atrophy in AD, the adjacent temporal horns undergo pronounced ex-vacuo dilation early in the disease course [@schoemaker2019]. Lateral ventricle expansion has therefore emerged as a sensitive structural biomarker for MCI and AD progression [@apostolova2013]. The rate of ventricular enlargement reliably differentiates healthy older adults from individuals with AD, and the steepest acceleration in ventricular expansion typically occurs at the point of clinical conversion from MCI to AD dementia [@madsen_mapping_2015].

The trajectory and magnitude of age-related ventricular expansion also show sex differences. Structural MRI studies consistently find that men have larger absolute and relative ventricular volumes than women across the adult lifespan, even after correcting for intracranial volume [@fjell_minute_2009; @pintzka_marked_2015]. Longitudinal and cross-sectional evidence indicates that ventricular expansion occurs at a faster rate and begins at an earlier age in men than in women [@voevodskaya_effects_2014]. Clinical assessments further show that abnormal ventricular enlargement becomes apparent in men, on average, six years earlier than in women, and men show a higher frequency of pathologically enlarged ventricles [@curra_ventricular_2019]. This sexual dimorphism in ventricular aging trajectories underscores the need to account for sex when using ventricular volume, or structural metrics derived from the adjacent hippocampus, as biomarkers for neurodegeneration.

## Structural MRI and Automated Segmentation

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the primary non-invasive method for quantifying human brain anatomy. High-resolution T1-weighted MRI is the standard sequence for structural volumetry due to its excellent inter-tissue contrast [@dadar2021bison; @alfaro-almagro_image_2018]. The T1 relaxation time reflects the duration required for 63% of perturbed protons to realign along the longitudinal axis of the main magnetic field, a property dictated by the motional frequencies of molecules within the local tissue environment [@dalaker2011]. In a T1-weighted image, protons bound in lipid-rich structures, such as myelin, recover rapidly and emit a strong signal, appearing bright. Conversely, freely moving protons in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) recover slowly and appear dark, resulting in images where white matter is distinctly hyperintense compared to the intermediate signal of cortical and subcortical gray matter, providing the sharp boundaries necessary for accurate morphological measurements [@dalaker2011].

### Manual Segmentation

Historically, the extraction of quantitative volumetric data from structural MRI relied entirely on manual segmentation. This approach remains the recognized "gold standard" against which all automated algorithms are validated [@amoroso2015; @zandifar2017]. In this process, expert neuroanatomists meticulously trace the boundaries of specific brain structures on a slice-by-slice basis. However, manual segmentation has major methodological and practical limitations. It is tedious and time-consuming, often requiring up to two hours to delineate a single complex structure like the hippocampus, and inherently subjective, being susceptible to intra-rater fatigue and inter-rater variability from differing boundary protocol interpretations [@dill2015; @yushkevich_quantitative_2015; @zandifar2017]. These drawbacks make manual segmentation impractical for modern, large-scale neuroimaging cohorts.

### Atlas-Based Methods

To overcome the bottleneck of manual tracing, automated segmentation methods were developed, initially relying heavily on atlas-based techniques. An atlas consists of a high-quality structural image paired with a "ground truth" label map. In standard model-based or single-atlas segmentation, a target MRI is spatially warped to match the atlas image using nonlinear registration, and the labels are then propagated back to the native target space using the inverse geometric transformation [@dill2015]. The Automatic Nonlinear Image Matching and Anatomical Labeling (ANIMAL) algorithm exemplifies this approach by operating in a multiscale, hierarchical fashion, estimating local 3D deformation fields to maximize the intensity correlation between the target and a previously labeled model brain [@collins1997; @collins1995]. While effective, single-atlas methods are ultimately limited because a single anatomical model cannot capture the full range of anatomical variability or disease-induced deformations [@zandifar2017].

To address the limitations of single-atlas approaches, Multi-Atlas Label Fusion (MALF) methods were introduced. Rather than relying on a single anatomical model, MALF registers a library of diverse, expertly labeled atlases to the target image using nonlinear registration algorithms such as ANIMAL, generating candidate segmentations whose combination mitigates the impact of individual registration failures or unrepresentative anatomy [@collins1997; @pipitone2014]. The final segmentation is computed using label fusion algorithms, which range from simple majority voting to more sophisticated, spatially weighted voting frameworks like Simultaneous Truth and Performance Level Estimation (STAPLE) or cross-correlation weighting [@pipitone2014; @zandifar2017]. While highly accurate, MALF requires performing dozens of computationally expensive nonlinear registrations for every new target image.

Non-Local Patch-Based (NLPB) segmentation later emerged as an alternative that relaxes the reliance on voxel-to-voxel macroscopic registration [@coupe2011]. Inspired by the non-local means filtering algorithm used for image denoising, NLPB methods estimate a target voxel's label by examining a small cubic volume (a patch) surrounding it. The algorithm searches a localized neighborhood within the atlas library for patches with similar intensity patterns. Labels are then fused using a weighted average, where the contribution of each atlas patch is directly proportional to its intensity-based similarity to the target patch [@coupe2011; @zandifar2017]. By comparing localized textures rather than relying exclusively on global shape warping, NLPB segmentation handles anatomical variation well and significantly reduces processing time, especially when combined with a pre-computed population-specific template [@fonov2012].

### Deep Learning Approaches

In recent years, deep learning has transformed biomedical image segmentation. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) process images through successive layers of learnable filters and nonlinear activation functions, automatically extracting hierarchical feature representations from raw image data without manual feature engineering or spatial registration [@xie2018]. The U-Net architecture, the most prominent CNN design for medical segmentation, features a symmetric encoder-decoder structure: the contracting encoder captures broad spatial context, while the expanding decoder enables precise localization, with skip connections concatenating high-resolution encoder features to upsampled decoder outputs to preserve fine structural details [@ronneberger2015]. Modern 3D implementations of these networks naturally process volumetric context and can perform full structural segmentations in a matter of seconds or minutes, offering a large improvement in computational efficiency over atlas-based techniques [@goubran2020; @xie2018].

![**The U-Net architecture for biomedical image segmentation.** The network comprises a contracting encoder path (left) that captures spatial context through successive convolutions and max-pooling operations, and an expanding decoder path (right) that enables precise localization through up-convolutions. Gray arrows denote skip connections that concatenate high-resolution feature maps from the encoder to the decoder, preserving fine structural details. From @ronneberger2015, CC BY 4.0.](../images/unet.pdf){#fig-unet width=90%}

### Validation Metrics

Evaluating automated segmentation algorithms relies on standardized metrics that compare the computed boundaries to manual ground-truth labels. The Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) is the most common metric, measuring volumetric spatial overlap as the size of the intersection of two segmentations divided by their average size, yielding a value between 0 (no overlap) and 1 (perfect agreement) [@dill2015; @pipitone2014]. Cohen's Kappa is similarly used to measure the agreement between categorical voxel assignments while formally correcting for the probability of chance agreement [@fleiss2003measurement; @zandifar2017]. Finally, to evaluate geometric precision, the Hausdorff distance measures the maximum distance from any point on the surface of the automated segmentation to the closest point on the ground-truth surface. Unlike volumetric overlap measures, the Hausdorff distance is highly sensitive to localized spatial outliers and shape deviations, making it a critical metric for evaluating the clinical fidelity of anatomical borders [@brusini2020; @goubran2020].

## Quality Control in Neuroimaging

Quality control (QC) is essential in neuroimaging pipelines, as structural MRI is susceptible to artifacts that can systematically bias morphometric analyses [@alexander2016subtle; @power2012spurious]. Artifacts often stem from participant motion (such as swallowing, blinking, chewing, or fidgeting), which generates blurring, ringing, and ghosting in the resulting images [@reuter_head_2015]. Technical artifacts, including radiofrequency noise, magnetic susceptibility, and intensity non-uniformity, also degrade image quality and obscure tissue boundaries [@sled1998]. Unaccounted-for motion and imaging artifacts can lead to spurious group differences, frequently mimicking gray matter atrophy and compromising derived measures of volume and cortical thickness [@reuter_head_2015]. These issues are particularly problematic in developmental and clinical populations, such as children or patients with neurodegenerative diseases, who are inherently more prone to head motion during scanning.

To systematically identify these sources of noise and bias, researchers have sought to establish objective, no-reference image quality metrics (IQMs). A foundational effort in this domain is the Quality Assessment Protocol (QAP), developed by the Preprocessed Connectomes Project, which computes structural metrics such as the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), foreground-to-background energy ratio (FBER), entropy focus criterion (EFC), voxel smoothness, and the percentage of artifact voxels [@shehzad2015preprocessed]. By quantifying noise and signal distributions, these IQMs provide standardized criteria for identifying suboptimal scans before they enter the processing stream.

Building upon the IQMs established by the QAP, fully automated machine learning tools have been developed to predict image quality. MRIQC automatically extracts 64 IQMs per structural image and uses a random forests classifier to yield a binary quality prediction, though its generalization to unseen scanning sites may require retraining [@esteban2017mriqc]. BrainQCNet [@garcia2022brainqcnet] addresses the need for rapid localized assessment using a deep learning attention-based model that classifies 2D slices in approximately one minute per scan, offering both global and localized artifact predictions that enable researchers to retain usable portions of partially corrupted scans.

QC requirements differ substantially between raw image assessment and the evaluation of derived processing outputs. Raw-image QC focuses on detecting acquisition-level artifacts (motion, noise, coverage gaps, intensity inhomogeneity) that may render a scan unsuitable for any downstream analysis. In contrast, derived-measure QC evaluates whether specific post-processing steps have been executed correctly: whether stereotaxic registration has accurately aligned the brain to a standard template, whether tissue classification has correctly delineated gray matter, white matter, and CSF, and whether subcortical segmentations faithfully capture the boundaries of target structures [@raamana2023visualqc]. Each processing stage introduces its own failure modes, and a scan that passes raw-image QC may still produce erroneous derived measures if, for example, intensity inhomogeneity leads to tissue misclassification or atypical anatomy causes registration errors [@sled1998; @reuter_head_2015].

While initial QC of raw images is critical, quality must also be rigorously assessed after subsequent post-processing steps, such as stereotaxic registration and tissue segmentation. For example, DARQ (Deep Automated Registration QC) employs a deep neural network (ResNet-18) to automatically evaluate the quality of linear stereotaxic registration to the MNI-ICBM 152 template, replacing the need for human raters to visually inspect spatial alignment [@fonov2022darq]. For tissue segmentation, the FreeSurfer Euler number, a quantitative measure of the topological complexity of the reconstructed cortical surface, has been identified as an excellent proxy for data quality, consistently outperforming metrics derived from raw images or functional motion tracking in identifying unusable scans [@rosen2018quantitative]. Furthermore, Qoala-T builds upon FreeSurfer outputs by using a supervised-learning random forests model to predict segmentation quality, utilizing structural measures like surface holes and white matter hypointensities to flag segmentations requiring manual review [@klapwijk2019].

The QC landscape for subcortical structures presents distinct challenges compared to cortical surface reconstruction. While cortical QC benefits from topological metrics like the Euler number and surface-based visualization tools, subcortical segmentation QC (for structures such as the hippocampus, amygdala, and ventricles) typically relies on visual inspection of label overlays on native-space images [@samann_freesurferbased_2020]. Errors in subcortical segmentation are often focal and structure-specific: the hippocampal boundary may bleed into the adjacent amygdala or parahippocampal gyrus, the choroid plexus may be misclassified as hippocampal tissue, or the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle may be incompletely captured [@wisse_critical_2014]. These errors are particularly difficult to detect without targeted visual review and can introduce systematic biases in volumetric analyses, especially when they correlate with clinical status (e.g., patients with greater atrophy are more likely to have ambiguous tissue boundaries).

The challenge of QC is amplified at the scale of modern population neuroimaging studies. Biobank-sized datasets, such as the UK Biobank (>50,000 brain scans), the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), or the Canadian Open Neuroscience Platform, generate volumes of imaging data that far exceed the capacity of traditional QC workflows [@miller_multimodal_2016; @alfaro-almagro_image_2018]. Manually inspecting every scan at every processing stage is infeasible when tens of thousands of subjects each require QC for raw image quality, registration, and multiple segmentation outputs. This "QC bottleneck" has created an acute need for collaborative QC platforms that can distribute the inspection workload across multiple raters while maintaining consistent rating standards and centralized data management. The development of such a platform, addressing the gap between existing tools and the demands of large-scale multi-step QC, is the subject of Chapter 3.

Despite the proliferation of automated QC tools, manual visual inspection remains the gold standard for neuroimaging quality control [@monereo2021quality]. Automated algorithms and classifiers often fail to accurately classify borderline cases or pathology that violates normal anatomical assumptions. Studies frequently recommend that automated tools be used to triage data, while scans assigned midrange quality probabilities strictly require manual inspection and potential editing [@klapwijk2019]. Errors in automated brain surface reconstruction or subcortical segmentation are inevitable, and human visual assessment is necessary to confirm that anatomical boundaries correspond correctly to the underlying MRI signal, correcting idiosyncratic issues like skull stripping failures or tissue misclassification [@monereo2021quality].

To facilitate manual review, several software platforms have been developed to streamline visual inspection and collaborative quality control. VisualQC is an extensible medical imaging software library designed to reduce the burden of manual QC by presenting composite visualizations for structural scans, segmentations, and registrations, while tracking user ratings and outlier alerts [@raamana2023visualqc]. Similarly, Mindcontrol is a web-based dashboard that links group-level descriptive statistics to individual 3D volume views, allowing researchers to collaboratively organize, annotate, and edit FreeSurfer segmentations in a centralized database [@keshavan2018mindcontrol]. However, traditional manual QC in many laboratories still frequently relies on assembling disparate, non-integrated software components (such as standalone image viewers paired with shared spreadsheets), which is inefficient and prone to clerical errors [@keshavan2018mindcontrol]. While tools like Mindcontrol and VisualQC address specific software niches, there remains a gap for a web platform for multi-rater visual QC across processing steps, independent of specific neuroimaging pipelines.

## Head-Size Normalization and Methodological Artifacts

Quantifying structural neurodegeneration or anatomical differences between populations is complicated by natural inter-subject variability in head size. Correcting regional brain volumes for variations in total intracranial volume (ICV) is therefore considered an essential methodological step in neuroimaging studies [@obrien_statistical_2011]. This correction is particularly important when investigating sexual dimorphism, as males possess, on average, a 10% to 12% larger total ICV than females across the lifespan [@brzezinski-rittner_disentangling_2025; @ruigrok_meta-analysis_2014; @voevodskaya_effects_2014]. Because most local brain structures scale positively with global cranial capacity, using raw, unadjusted volumes confounds the specific effects of sex or localized pathology with the generic effects of overall body and head size [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020].

To mitigate this variance, researchers generally employ one of four primary analytical methods. The first is to simply use _unadjusted_ raw volumes, which preserves natural anatomical variation but fails entirely to address head-size confounds [@nordenskjold_intracranial_2015; @voevodskaya_effects_2014]. The second is the _proportions_ method, which calculates a "brain fraction" by dividing the absolute volume of the region of interest by the individual's total ICV [@obrien_statistical_2011; @sanfilipo_correction_2004]. The third is the _residualization_ (or ANCOVA/covariate) method, which uses linear regression to estimate the association between ICV and regional volume; adjusted volumes are then calculated using the residuals of this regression (e.g., $Volume_{adjusted} = Volume_{raw} - \beta \times (ICV_{raw} - ICV_{mean})$), rendering the resulting outcome measure statistically uncorrelated with ICV [@voevodskaya_effects_2014]. Finally, _stereotaxic normalization_ (or scaling) corrects for head size by warping individual brain scans into a standard template space, scaling the local volumes based on the non-linear determinants of the spatial transformation matrix [@collins1995; @sanchis-segura_effects_2020].

The discrepancy in results across these methods largely stems from their underlying mathematical assumptions about brain geometry, specifically the concept of allometric scaling. The proportions method strictly assumes _isometric_ scaling: the premise that a regional brain structure grows in perfect, 1:1 proportion to total brain size, such that a regression line plotting the structure against ICV would pass directly through the origin [@de_jong_allometric_2017; @pintzka_marked_2015]. However, human brain structures scale _allometrically_ with ICV, and subcortical structures including the hippocampus are hypoallometric, meaning their volume increases at a slower rate than overall ICV [@de_jong_allometric_2017; @williams_neuroanatomical_2021]. Because the y-intercept of the true hippocampus-to-ICV relationship is not zero, utilizing the simple proportions method systematically over-corrects individuals with smaller ICVs (predominantly females) and under-corrects those with larger ICVs (predominantly males) [@pintzka_marked_2015; @sanchis-segura_effects_2020].

The degree of allometric deviation varies across brain structures and is not captured by a single correction factor. Allometric exponents, the power-law coefficients relating regional volume to ICV in the form $V_{\text{region}} \propto \text{ICV}^b$, differ by structure: cortical gray matter scales nearly isometrically ($b \approx 1.0$), while subcortical nuclei like the hippocampus and caudate show strongly hypoallometric exponents ($b \approx 0.5$--$0.7$), and the lateral ventricles are hyperallometric ($b > 1.0$), expanding disproportionately in larger brains [@de_jong_allometric_2017; @williams_neuroanatomical_2021]. This heterogeneity means that no single proportional or linear correction can simultaneously produce unbiased estimates for all brain regions. Stereotaxic normalization partially addresses this limitation by applying spatially varying deformation fields that adapt locally to each brain region's morphology, avoiding the assumption of a single global scaling factor and better accommodating the heterogeneous allometric relationships across structures [@collins1995].

This artifact has major consequences for the brain morphometry literature, producing contradictory conclusions from the same data. When evaluating sex differences in the hippocampus, the estimated effect can shift dramatically depending on the analytical choice. Unadjusted volume comparisons suggest a large male advantage ($d = -0.89$), but the proportions method reverses this finding to a spurious female advantage ($d = +0.58$), a swing driven by the mathematical over-correction of smaller female heads rather than actual tissue differences [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020]. When residualization is applied to remove the shared variance of ICV, the apparent sex differences often vanish, revealing no significant structural disparity between male and female hippocampi once head size is properly handled [@obrien_statistical_2011; @pintzka_marked_2015; @voevodskaya_effects_2014].

Despite clear evidence of the biases associated with techniques like the proportions method [@wang_comparison_2024], there is no consensus on the optimal approach for head-size normalization [@nordenskjold_intracranial_2015; @obrien_statistical_2011]. Much of the literature on structural sexual dimorphism or early regional atrophy remains method-dependent [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020; @voevodskaya_effects_2014]. Conclusions about which brain structures are "larger" or "smaller" across populations often reflect the chosen statistical artifact rather than biological reality, underscoring the need for self-normalizing morphometric indices that can avoid the assumptions of mathematical ICV adjustments [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020].

## The Hippocampal-to-Ventricle Ratio

Quantifying medial temporal lobe atrophy is complicated by large inter-subject variability in baseline brain volumes, making it difficult to distinguish a congenitally small hippocampus from one undergoing active neurodegeneration [@heister2011; @lupien2007]. To address this, researchers began exploiting the physiological principle of _ex vacuo_ dilation, the process by which cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces passively expand to fill the void left by shrinking parenchymal tissue. Building on this concept, the Hippocampal Occupancy (HOC) score was developed as an early composite structural biomarker, calculated as the ratio of hippocampal volume to the sum of hippocampal and adjacent inferior lateral ventricle volumes, and proved superior to standard normalized hippocampal volumes in predicting conversion from MCI to AD [@heister2011].

Building on the HOC score, the Hippocampal-to-Ventricle Ratio (HVR) was introduced to provide a more comprehensive cross-sectional estimation of hippocampal structural integrity [@schoemaker2019]. A key computational distinction between the two measures lies in the CSF compartment each captures. The HOC score is restricted to the inferior lateral ventricle (temporal horn) volume, reflecting only the most immediate fluid space adjacent to the hippocampus [@heister2011]. The HVR, by contrast, encompasses the full perihippocampal CSF envelope (including the temporal horn, uncal recess, hippocampal fissure, and portions of the quadrigeminal cistern), thereby capturing a broader set of fluid compartments that respond to hippocampal tissue loss [@schoemaker2019]. This wider CSF definition increases the measure's sensitivity to early atrophic changes that may not yet produce visible temporal horn dilation.

It is defined by the formula: HVR = HCvol / (HCvol + CSFvol), where HCvol represents the absolute volume of the hippocampus and CSFvol represents the volume of the perihippocampal CSF [@schoemaker2019]. The resulting ratio yields a value between 0 and 1. A value approaching 1 indicates preserved hippocampal tissue with minimal volume loss and very small surrounding ventricles, whereas lower values approaching 0 indicate severe structural atrophy and pronounced ventricular expansion [@schoemaker2019].

![**The Hippocampal-to-Ventricle Ratio (HVR).** Coronal T1-weighted MRI showing the hippocampus (HC, red) and surrounding perihippocampal cerebrospinal fluid compartments (CSF, blue). The HVR is computed as the ratio of hippocampal volume to the combined volume of the hippocampus and adjacent CSF. Adapted from @schoemaker2019.](../images/HVR.png){#fig-hvr-diagram width=60%}

The HVR is approximately self-normalizing with respect to head size. In standard morphometric studies, correcting raw regional volumes for total intracranial volume (ICV) is an essential but debated methodological step, as different mathematical adjustments (such as proportional division or regression-based residuals) carry different statistical assumptions and can alter study outcomes [@obrien_statistical_2011; @pintzka_marked_2015; @sanfilipo_correction_2004]. Because both the hippocampus and the adjacent ventricles scale positively with overall intracranial volume, their ratio effectively minimizes the shared variance associated with global head size. The HVR therefore adjusts for pre-morbid head size without requiring external ICV-correction algorithms, isolating atrophic change from normal anatomical diversity. Formally, if both HCvol and CSFvol scale with ICV by a common factor $k$ (i.e., $\text{HCvol} \propto k \cdot \text{ICV}$ and $\text{CSFvol} \propto k \cdot \text{ICV}$), then the ratio $\text{HCvol} / (\text{HCvol} + \text{CSFvol})$ algebraically cancels the ICV-dependent scaling, yielding a dimensionless index that reflects the relative tissue-to-fluid composition of the medial temporal lobe independent of absolute cranial size. This cancellation is exact under isometric scaling and approximately holds even under mild allometric departures, making the ratio more robust to head-size confounds than either raw volumes or single-structure proportional adjustments.

Two large-scale neuroimaging datasets are central to the empirical validation and application of the HVR across this thesis. The UK Biobank (UKB) is a prospective population-based cohort of approximately 500,000 participants aged 40--69 at recruitment, of whom over 50,000 have undergone brain MRI [@miller_multimodal_2016; @alfaro-almagro_image_2018]. The UKB provides the normative, population-scale dataset needed to characterize the HVR's distributional properties, establish sex-stratified reference norms, and evaluate its self-normalizing claims in a demographically diverse, largely cognitively healthy sample (Chapter 5). The Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) is a longitudinal multi-site study specifically designed to track biomarker changes across the AD continuum, enrolling cognitively healthy controls, individuals with MCI, and patients with AD dementia [@jack_alzheimers_2008]. ADNI provides the clinical, longitudinal dataset needed to validate the automated HVR against manual segmentation (Chapter 4) and to test whether normative models derived from the UKB transfer to a disease-enriched population and whether HVR trajectories predict cognitive decline and mediate cardiovascular risk effects (Chapter 6).

Preliminary evidence indicates that the HVR outperforms standard hippocampal volumetry even in cognitively normal aging populations. In a validation study of two independent cohorts of healthy older adults, the HVR yielded stronger negative associations with age than raw hippocampal volumes [@schoemaker2019]. Unlike raw hippocampal volume, whose relationship with memory in healthy aging is often inconsistent [@vanpetten2004], the HVR consistently emerged as a significant predictor of delayed recall memory performance across both cohorts, whereas standard hippocampal volume failed to reach significance in one [@schoemaker2019].

Despite these initial results, several properties of the HVR remain unknown. The foundational HVR studies relied on small, cross-sectional samples (cohorts of 50 and 88 individuals) using labor-intensive manual segmentation, which limits generalizability [@schoemaker2019]. It remains to be determined how the HVR behaves in population-scale datasets and whether its normative properties can be characterized across diverse demographics. Furthermore, while the HVR's self-normalizing nature is theoretically advantageous, it has not been formally evaluated against the standard statistical adjustment methods to confirm its superiority in handling neuroanatomical confounds like sex and head size. Finally, clinical validation requires longitudinal data to determine whether baseline HVR or its trajectory over time can predict individual cognitive decline and disease progression across the neurodegenerative continuum [@schoemaker2019]. The development of an automated HVR computation pipeline and its validation against manual segmentation and conventional hippocampal volumetry is the subject of Chapter 4.

## Sex Differences in Brain Aging

Human brain structure shows well-documented sexual dimorphism across the lifespan. On a macroscopic scale, males generally have approximately 10% to 12% larger total brain volume and ICV than females, corresponding to larger absolute raw volumes across most subcortical structures and greater total cortical surface area, while females consistently show higher average cortical thickness, particularly in the parietal and frontal lobes [@ritchie_sex_2018; @ruigrok_meta-analysis_2014].

However, the interpretation of these structural sex differences remains controversial, largely because findings depend on the methodological approaches used to adjust for head size [@pintzka_marked_2015; @sanchis-segura_effects_2020]. As noted above, unadjusted raw volumes make males appear to have much larger brain structures. Proportional corrections (dividing regional volume by ICV) over-correct female brains due to hypoallometric scaling of subcortical structures, producing spurious female volumetric advantages [@nordenskjold_intracranial_2015; @pintzka_marked_2015]. When residualization or ICV-matching is applied, many of these apparent regional sex differences vanish or are reduced to small effect sizes [@pintzka_marked_2015; @ritchie_sex_2018]. Multivariate sex prediction from brain features drops from over 80% accuracy using raw data to roughly 60% after ICV control [@sanchis-segura_effects_2020], indicating that many reported sex differences are statistical artifacts of overall size rather than genuine sexual dimorphism.

Beyond baseline structural size, the trajectories of brain aging also differ by sex. Structural decline over time does not occur uniformly between the sexes; evidence indicates that older males show steeper rates of subcortical volume loss than females [@ritchie_sex_2018]. Most prominently, lateral ventricle expansion begins earlier and progresses more rapidly in men, with abnormal ventricular enlargement becoming apparent on average six years earlier than in women and preferentially affecting the frontal horns [@curra_ventricular_2019]. These sex-differential aging trajectories underscore the need to account for sex when using morphological markers of neurodegeneration.

Structural brain metrics do not predict cognitive abilities equally across the sexes [@jockwitz_differential_2024]. In older adults, global brain networks and regional gray matter volumes predict cognitive profiles with different strength and spatial specificity; males appear to rely on a more integrative, global cognitive processing network, whereas female cognitive processing tends to be more segregated into specialized local subsystems [@jockwitz_differential_2024].

This differential coupling is particularly evident in the relationship between the hippocampus and memory function. While the hippocampus is critical for relational binding and associative memory, its volume predicts memory performance differently in men versus women. In cognitively normal older adults, larger hippocampal gray matter volume predicts better associative memory in women, but this structure-function coupling is absent in men [@zheng_sex_2017]. Furthermore, women maintain a behavioral advantage in verbal memory tasks over men, even in the presence of MCI and similar levels of hippocampal atrophy or temporal hypometabolism [@sundermann_female_2016]. This female advantage is thought to represent a sex-specific form of cognitive reserve that delays observable memory decline until pathology reaches a more advanced threshold [@sundermann_female_2016].

The influence of sex on both baseline brain structure and age-related atrophy trajectories underscores the need for sex-specific normative reference values. The recent "brain charting" movement has aggregated large global neuroimaging datasets to establish standardized lifespan growth and aging curves for brain morphometry, analogous to pediatric growth charts, enabling researchers to quantify how far an individual's brain morphology deviates from healthy aging expectations [@bethlehem_brain_2022].

To map these lifespan trajectories, researchers employ Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS) as the statistical framework [@bethlehem_brain_2022; @dima_subcortical_2022]. GAMLSS is well suited for brain charting because it simultaneously models non-linear age-related trends in the mean (location) while also capturing changes in population variance (scale) and skewness (shape) across time [@bethlehem_brain_2022]. Because male and female aging trajectories differ, and because males show greater inter-subject structural variability than females across the lifespan [@ritchie_sex_2018; @williams_neuroanatomical_2021], sex-stratified GAMLSS centiles are needed to avoid misclassifying healthy anatomical diversity as neurodegeneration.

![**Brain charts for the human lifespan.** Sex-stratified normative reference curves (red: female; blue: male) for cerebrum tissue volumes across the lifespan, modeled using GAMLSS. (b) Raw data with centile curves for gray matter, white matter, subcortical gray matter, and ventricular volume. (c) Normative trajectories showing median and centile bands. (d) Normative variance across age. (e) Normative rate of growth (mm$^3$ per day). Note the pronounced sex differences in ventricular volume trajectories and the widening variance in older age. From @bethlehem_brain_2022, CC BY 4.0.](../images/brain_charts.png){#fig-brain-charts width=100%}

The biological mechanisms driving these structural and cognitive sex differences are multifactorial, involving lifetime exposure to sex steroid hormones. Estrogens, particularly estradiol, exert neuroprotective and neurotrophic effects including hippocampal neurogenesis, synaptic plasticity, and reduced neuroinflammation, such that reproductive milestones determining cumulative estrogen exposure (menarche, menopause, parity) affect gray matter volume and estimated brain age later in life [@de_lange_womens_2020; @jett_endogenous_2022; @luders_case_2025]. The menopausal transition, characterized by a sharp drop in estrogen, represents a window of neurological vulnerability that may accelerate structural brain aging and AD risk [@jett_endogenous_2022].

Genetic risk factors for neurodegeneration, most notably the apolipoprotein E (APOE) ε4 allele, also interact with biological sex to modulate brain aging and disease risk. The APOE ε4 allele carries a stronger pathological impact in females, conferring greater risk for Alzheimer's disease than in male carriers [@ferretti_sex_2018]. In prodromal stages such as amnestic MCI, female APOE ε4 carriers show faster longitudinal hippocampal atrophy and more rapid cognitive decline than their male counterparts [@park_sex-specific_2025]. Additionally, cognitively normal female APOE ε4 carriers show increased tau deposition within the medial temporal lobe compared to males with similar amyloid burdens [@buckley_sex_2019]. This gene-by-sex interaction highlights how sex-specific vulnerabilities converge with genetic risk to alter the trajectory of brain aging, further supporting the need for sex-stratified models in neuroimaging research. Chapter 5 addresses this need by evaluating the HVR's self-normalizing properties with respect to head size and sex, establishing sex-specific normative aging curves, and characterizing brain-cognition coupling in males and females at the population scale.

## Cardiovascular Risk and Brain Health

The trajectory of cognitive decline and the risk of developing AD are not determined solely by genetic factors and chronological age. Approximately 35% of global dementia cases are potentially attributable to modifiable cardiovascular risk (CVR) factors including hypertension, obesity, diabetes, and smoking, which frequently co-occur and exert compounding effects on vascular and metabolic health, making cumulative cardiovascular risk burden one of the most important modifiable pathways for dementia prevention [@livingston_dementia_2017].

To capture this cumulative cardiovascular burden, epidemiological and clinical research frequently employs the Framingham General Cardiovascular Risk Score (FGCRS or FRS). Originally developed to predict 10-year cardiovascular event risk, the FRS integrates chronological age, sex, systolic blood pressure, antihypertensive medication use, total and HDL cholesterol, smoking status, and diabetes into a single weighted composite score [@dagostino_general_2008]. Because it combines interacting physiological variables into a single metric, the FRS has been widely adopted beyond cardiology to study the impact of vascular health on the aging brain [@kaffashian_predictive_2011].

A growing body of literature shows that an elevated FRS is associated with both structural brain changes and accelerated cognitive decline. Higher cardiovascular risk burdens are associated with reduced total cerebral brain volume, smaller hippocampal volume, and increased white matter hyperintensities [@seshadri_stroke_2004; @song_associations_2020], while longitudinally, an adverse Framingham risk profile predicts steeper decline in executive function, working memory, perceptual speed, and episodic memory, even in cohorts free of clinical stroke or overt dementia [@kaffashian_predictive_2011; @song_associations_2020]. Furthermore, midlife stroke risk has been shown to predict lower gray matter density in the medial temporal lobe and compromised fractional anisotropy in white matter tracts decades later [@zsoldos_association_2020].

Despite its predictive utility, using the FRS as a predictor of neurodegeneration in elderly cohorts presents a methodological challenge: the confounding effect of age. In the FRS algorithm, chronological age carries the heaviest mathematical weight, dominating the composite score's variance in older populations [@koller_development_2012; @pencina_quantifying_2019]. Because advancing age drives both the FRS calculation and, independently, neurodegeneration and cognitive decline, age acts as a common cause. When using the raw FRS to predict brain changes in the elderly, the apparent pathway from cardiovascular risk to brain atrophy may largely reflect the passage of time. Furthermore, entering age as a covariate in standard regression models does not adequately resolve this issue; because age is embedded within the FRS calculation, regressing it out leads to over-adjustment and collinearity, obscuring the true magnitude of age-independent cardiovascular effects [@koller_development_2012; @pencina_quantifying_2019].

The impact of cardiovascular risk and age on clinical outcomes is rooted in the concept of "brain-cognition coupling," the phenomenon whereby changes in brain structure correspond to trajectories of cognitive performance [@oschwald_brain_2020]. This structural-functional coupling is clinically predictive: longitudinal hippocampal shrinkage independently predicts subsequent declines in episodic memory and executive function in healthy older adults [@kramer_longitudinal_2007]. Understanding how external risk factors such as cumulative cardiovascular burden accelerate this correlated change between structural atrophy and cognitive decline is a central goal of cognitive aging research [@oschwald_brain_2020].

The relationship between brain atrophy and cognitive decline is not uniform across individuals; it is moderated by reserve. Stern's framework distinguishes between "brain reserve," a passive structural capacity (such as larger intracranial volume or higher synaptic density) that allows the brain to tolerate more pathology before a clinical threshold is crossed, and "cognitive reserve," an active functional construct representing the brain's ability to optimize or recruit compensatory neural pathways to maintain performance despite structural degradation [@stern_cognitive_2012]. Factors like higher education, occupational complexity, and the absence of severe cardiovascular burden can preserve cognitive reserve, buffering the clinical effects of age-related brain atrophy.

The interplay between cardiovascular risk, brain aging, and reserve is also modified by biological sex [@ferretti_sex_2018]. Men and women show different lifelong cardiovascular risk profiles, with men generally experiencing higher rates of coronary heart disease in midlife, while women face escalating risk of stroke, heart failure, and hypertension following the menopausal transition [@ferretti_sex_2018]. This shift is influenced by the loss of endogenous estrogens, particularly estradiol, which normally exert neuroprotective, anti-inflammatory, and cardioprotective effects during a woman's reproductive years [@jett_endogenous_2022]. These sex-specific physiological environments also interact with genetic risk factors. The APOE ε4 allele, the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset AD, confers a higher pathological burden, faster structural atrophy, and greater risk of dementia in females than in males [@ferretti_sex_2018; @jett_endogenous_2022]. The convergence of post-menopausal estrogen depletion, distinct cardiovascular aging trajectories, and heightened genetic vulnerability underscores the need to consider sex differences when evaluating how cardiovascular risk impacts brain health across the lifespan. Chapter 6 investigates whether cardiovascular risk, as measured by the FRS, mediates hippocampal-cognitive decline along the AD continuum, and introduces an age-adjustment framework to disentangle cardiovascular effects from the confounding influence of age.

## Analytical Framework

The biological questions outlined above require statistical tools capable of handling latent constructs, longitudinal trajectories, and multi-group comparisons. This section introduces the analytical methods employed across the thesis: mixed-effects models (Chapter 6), distributional regression for normative charting (Chapters 5 and 6), and structural equation modeling and its extensions (Chapters 5 and 6).

### Linear Mixed-Effects Models

Linear Mixed-Effects (LME) models, also known as multilevel or hierarchical linear models, provide a framework for analyzing longitudinal and nested data. LME models decompose variance into "fixed effects," which estimate the population-average relationship between predictors and the outcome, and "random effects," which capture subject-specific deviations from these average trajectories, allowing each individual to have their own starting point (random intercept) and rate of change (random slope) [@bates_fitting_2015; @grimm_growth_2016; @rajagopal_estimating_2024].

LME models offer advantages over traditional repeated-measures ANOVA for longitudinal data due to their flexibility with unbalanced data structures. While ANOVA requires complete data and fixed measurement intervals (using listwise deletion for missing time points), LME models rely on Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) estimation, permitting inclusion of participants with missing visits, unequal numbers of observations, and varying intervals between assessments, maximizing statistical power and avoiding biased sample attrition [@grimm_growth_2016; @rajagopal_estimating_2024; @ducharme2016trajectories].

This framework is well suited for testing longitudinal moderation, such as the modulation of brain-cognition coupling. By specifying a three-way interaction term (for example, Time $\times$ Covariate $\times$ Brain Structure), researchers can test whether the slope of cognitive decline, as predicted by structural brain atrophy, is steeper or shallower depending on a secondary risk factor like cardiovascular burden [@bollen_latent_2006]. The random slopes handle the temporal dependency of the repeated measures, while the fixed interaction terms capture how external variables alter the magnitude of structural-functional coupling over time.

Chapter 6 uses LME models to test a three-way interaction (Time $\times$ CVR $\times$ HVR) in the ADNI longitudinal cohort, evaluating whether cardiovascular risk moderates the coupling between hippocampal atrophy and cognitive decline.

### GAMLSS and Normative Centile Modeling

Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS) is a flexible statistical framework designed for generating normative reference charts. While traditional linear or additive models estimate changes only in the mean of a distribution, GAMLSS permits simultaneous, non-linear modeling of up to four distribution moments: the mean (location), variance (scale), skewness (shape), and kurtosis [@rigby_generalized_2005; @bethlehem_brain_2022].

Modeling variance and skewness is important for lifespan biological data. Inter-individual variability in brain structure changes across the lifespan, typically widening in older age groups as varied trajectories of atrophy unfold [@dima_subcortical_2022]. GAMLSS handles these shifts using flexible distribution families (such as the fractional polynomial or generalized gamma distributions) and can incorporate random effects to harmonize scanner- or site-specific "batch effects" common in large neuroimaging datasets [@bethlehem_brain_2022].

In the context of normative brain charting, GAMLSS constructs age- and sex-specific centile curves, analogous to pediatric growth charts. By plotting an individual's structural MRI metrics against these population-level normative curves, researchers can extract standardized centile scores or z-scores. These scores quantify how far an individual's brain morphometry deviates from the expected healthy median for their age and sex, providing a sensitive biomarker for neurodegeneration [@bethlehem_brain_2022].

Chapters 5 and 6 both use GAMLSS to construct sex-stratified normative centile curves for brain measures: Chapter 5 establishes the UK Biobank reference norms, and Chapter 6 transfers these norms to the ADNI clinical cohort.

### Structural Equation Modeling

Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) is a multivariate statistical framework that unifies multiple regression, path analysis, and factor analysis [@bollen_structural_1989; @newsom_longitudinal_2015]. SEM models relationships among observed (manifest) variables, which are directly measured, and latent variables, which are unobserved constructs inferred from the data. By explicitly modeling measurement error, SEM estimates the "true" relationships among constructs, yielding more accurate parameter estimates than standard regression approaches that assume perfect measurement.

SEMs are frequently represented using path diagrams, in which squares or rectangles denote observed variables, circles or ellipses represent latent variables, single-headed arrows indicate directional regression effects, and double-headed arrows indicate correlations or covariances [@bollen_structural_1989; @newsom_longitudinal_2015].

![**Example of a Structural Equation Model (SEM) path diagram.** Two latent variables (circles), Intelligence and Academic Performance, are measured by their respective observed indicators (squares). Single-headed arrows represent directional regression paths (factor loadings from latent to observed, and the structural path between latent variables), while small circles with double-headed arrows denote error (residual) variance terms. By Tim Bates, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.](../images/SEM_example.png){#fig-sem-example width=80%}

The SEM framework consists of two submodels: the measurement model, which defines how observed indicators map onto underlying latent variables through confirmatory factor analysis, and the structural model, which specifies the directional relationships among the latent variables themselves, allowing researchers to evaluate causal hypotheses and mediational pathways [@bollen_structural_1989].

SEM parameters are estimated by minimizing the discrepancy between the sample covariance matrix and the covariance matrix implied by the hypothesized model. Maximum Likelihood (ML) is the standard estimation method for continuous indicators, providing asymptotically unbiased estimates under multivariate normality [@bollen_structural_1989]. For categorical or ordinal indicators, robust weighted least squares estimators such as WLSMV (Weighted Least Squares Mean and Variance adjusted) account for non-normal distributions [@newsom_longitudinal_2015]. Model adequacy is evaluated using absolute and incremental fit indices. The Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) and the Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR) are absolute indices, where values $\le .06$ and $\le .08$, respectively, indicate good fit, while incremental indices such as the Comparative Fit Index (CFI) and the Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI) compare the model against a baseline null model, with values $\ge .95$ indicating excellent fit [@hu_cutoff_1999].

Chapters 5 and 6 use structural equation modeling to model brain-cognition structural paths.

### Confirmatory Factor Analysis and Bifactor Models

Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) serves as the foundational measurement component of the broader SEM framework. Unlike exploratory factor analysis, which allows all observed variables to load on all extracted factors, CFA requires the researcher to specify a strict, _a priori_ theoretical structure [@bollen_structural_1989]. In a CFA, paths from latent factors to observed variables (factor loadings) are constrained to zero where no theoretical relationship is expected, allowing for rigorous hypothesis testing regarding the underlying dimensionality of a measurement instrument [@newsom_longitudinal_2015].

For multidimensional constructs, the bifactor model provides an effective CFA specification. A bifactor model partitions the variance of observed indicators into two sources: a single general factor (the G-factor) that accounts for the shared variance among all items, and multiple orthogonal specific factors (S-factors) that account for residual variance shared among items within particular sub-domains [@eid_anomalous_2017; @burns_application_2020]. Because the specific factors are orthogonal (uncorrelated) to the general factor and to each other, the model separates global trait variance from domain-specific variance.

This partitioning makes the bifactor approach well suited for modeling constructs like general cognitive ability. In cognitive research, individuals complete a battery of distinct tasks (e.g., memory, executive function, language). A bifactor model isolates the variance common to all cognitive tasks, interpreted as global cognitive capacity, while simultaneously modeling the unique variances attributable to specific cognitive domains [@eid_anomalous_2017]. This provides better measurement precision than traditional higher-order factor models, ensuring that the general factor is defined by shared true-score variance without distortion from correlated sub-domains.

Chapter 5 employs a bifactor CFA to decompose the UK Biobank cognitive battery into a general cognitive factor and domain-specific factors, establishing the measurement model for brain--cognition SEM.

### Measurement Invariance

Before comparing latent variable means or structural paths across groups (e.g., males versus females), researchers must establish measurement invariance, ensuring that the underlying construct is measured identically across groups so that observed differences reflect true variations in the latent trait rather than measurement bias [@putnick_measurement_2016; @newsom_longitudinal_2015]. Testing for invariance involves a sequential process of increasingly restrictive multiple-group CFA models: (1) _configural invariance_ tests whether the same overall factor structure exists across groups; (2) _metric (weak) invariance_ constrains factor loadings to be equal, ensuring the unit of measurement is identical; (3) _scalar (strong) invariance_ constrains item intercepts, ensuring the origin of the scale is identical; and (4) _strict invariance_ constrains the residual variances, assuming the measurement error is identical across groups.

Because the standard $\chi^2$ difference test is overly sensitive to sample size, measurement invariance is typically evaluated using changes in practical fit indices between nested models. Simulation research has established thresholds for these changes: invariance is generally supported if equality constraints produce a decrease in CFI $\le .01$ ($\Delta CFI \le .01$) and an increase in RMSEA $\le .015$ ($\Delta RMSEA \le .015$) [@chen_sensitivity_2007; @cheung_evaluating_2002].

Establishing measurement invariance is a prerequisite for the cross-sex latent construct comparisons conducted in Chapter 5, and for the age-group comparisons of the CVR MIMIC model in Chapter 6.

### MIMIC Models

Multiple Indicators Multiple Causes (MIMIC) models are a form of SEM used to incorporate observed covariates directly into a latent variable measurement model [@bollen_structural_1989; @newsom_longitudinal_2015]. In a standard CFA, observed variables act only as _indicators_ (effects) of an underlying construct; a MIMIC model extends this by allowing external observed variables (such as sex, education, or age) to act as _causes_ (predictors) of the latent factor.

By treating a covariate like chronological age as a direct cause of a latent risk factor, the MIMIC model partitions the variance of the construct. The structural regression removes the variance attributable to the covariate, leaving a residual term that represents the construct orthogonal to the covariate [@joreskog_estimation_1975; @bollen_structural_1989]. Factor scores extracted from this residual variance represent a refined metric (e.g., cardiovascular risk) that is free of age-related confounding, enabling the isolation of pathological effects from the passage of time.

Chapter 6 employs a MIMIC model to extract an age-adjusted latent cardiovascular risk factor ($\text{CVR}_{\text{mimic}}$) from the Framingham Risk Score components, resolving the age-confounding problem discussed above.

### Latent Growth Curve Models

Latent Growth Curve Models (LGCM) represent an advanced application of SEM used to model longitudinal change. In an LGCM, repeated measures of a variable over time act as indicators for underlying latent factors representing the trajectory of change. Typically, two latent growth factors are specified: a latent intercept, with factor loadings fixed to 1 to represent the baseline level of the construct, and a latent slope, with factor loadings fixed to values corresponding to the metric of time (e.g., 0, 1, 2, 3) to represent the individual rate of change [@bollen_latent_2006; @grimm_growth_2016].

LGCMs are preferred over traditional repeated-measures ANOVA because they capture inter-individual differences in intra-individual change. Rather than assessing only group-level mean differences over time, LGCMs estimate the variance of the latent intercept and slope, quantifying how much individuals differ in their starting points and rates of change. Because LGCMs operate within the SEM framework, they handle missing data via FIML estimation, accommodate non-linear trajectories, and allow the latent change factors to be used as predictors or outcomes in broader causal models [@bollen_latent_2006; @grimm_growth_2016].

An important extension is the parallel-process (or bivariate) LGCM, which models two longitudinal trajectories simultaneously (e.g., structural brain volume and cognitive performance) [@muniz-terrera_latent_2017; @bollen_latent_2006]. By estimating covariance or directional regression paths between the latent growth factors of both processes, researchers can evaluate dynamic temporal mediation. A predictor variable can be modeled to influence the latent slope of the first process (e.g., the rate of brain atrophy), which in turn predicts the latent slope of the second process (e.g., the rate of cognitive decline), establishing longitudinal mediation through this "slope-to-slope" structural path.

Chapter 6 extends the LME framework with parallel-process LGCMs, modeling the simultaneous longitudinal trajectories of hippocampal atrophy and cognitive decline to test whether cardiovascular risk mediates brain--cognition coupling.
